# Bālapaṇḍita Sutta (MN 129 (PTS MN iii 163))
**ID:** MN 129 (PTS MN iii 163)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)

**Title (Pali):** Bālapaṇḍita Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Foolish and the Astute

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta* (MN 129) is a discourse in the *Majjhimanikāya* examining the karmic consequences experienced by the foolish person (*bāla*) and the wise or astute person (*paṇḍita*) [SuttaCentral; Collins 1998; Marino 2017]. The text expounds how a fool who commits misdeeds of body, speech, and mind experiences three kinds of immediate torment in the present life—social disapproval, a guilty conscience, and terror of judicial punishment and graphic physical torture—before undergoing severe bodily torments in hell or rebirth as an animal [Collins 1998; Radich 2007]. Hell is characterized as an experience that is "utterly unwished for, utterly undesired, utterly disagreeable" [Goodman 2009; Marino 2017]. Conversely, the astute person engages in wholesome conduct, enjoys immediate ease and protection, and is reborn in heaven, an abode described as "utterly wished for, utterly desired, utterly agreeable" [Collins 1998; Goodman 2009]. In illustrating royal majesty and divine bliss, the sutta provides an extensive treatment of the seven treasures (*ratana*) and four blessings of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) [Meisig 2010; Thanissaro 1996].
Scholars note that MN 129 stands alongside the adjacent *Devadūta Sutta* (MN 130) as one of the foundational early cosmographical descriptions of heaven and hell [Marino 2017; Thanissaro 1996]. In modern text-critical analysis, comparative studies suggest that the detailed portrayal of the wheel-turning king's treasures represents an expansion specific to the Pali transmission, as its *Madhyama-āgama* counterpart preserves only a brief enumeration [Meisig 2010]. In another passage describing the fool's regret, parallels in the *Madhyama-āgama*, the Chinese *Nili jing* (T 86), and the Sanskrit *Śrāvakabhūmi* explicitly mention the fool falling sick, indicating that MN 129 likely lost this reference to illness and retained only a description of lying down to rest [Anālayo 2016].
Curated parallels include *Madhyama-āgama* discourse MĀ 199, an independent Chinese translation titled *Nili jing* (T 86, which combines material from MN 129 and MN 130), a Sanskrit Vinaya text (*lo-mvu2*), and the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (Up 2.033) [SuttaCentral; Marino 2017]. Computer-assisted analysis by DharmaNexus corroborates extensive text reuse with MĀ 199 (T 26.53), T 86, and the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, while also recording substantial cross-language alignments with the *Lalitavistara* and *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus identifies significant shared material with the *Devadūta Sutta* (MN 130), the *Mahāsudassana Sutta* (DN 17) and *Cakkavatti Sutta* (DN 26) regarding the monarch's treasures, as well as multiple sections across the *Aṅguttaranikāya* [DharmaNexus].
